Neonates of Gould, or Parasuta gouldii, emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length of 13 cm [Lb = 13 cm], placing them among the smaller offspring within the elapid radiation. This modest size at hatching is accompanied by a neonatal body mass of 3.5 g [Wwb = 3.5 g], a value that reflects the finite yolk reserves allocated to each embryo prior to oviposition. The transition to exogenous feeding typically occurs within the first few weeks following eclosion, during which the yolk-sac larva completes the absorption of internal nutrients. Foraging behavior in these young individuals is characterized by an ambush strategy targeting small skinks, and the initial growth trajectory is relatively rapid. Available records indicate that females attain reproductive maturity at a snout-vent length of 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm], whereas males undergo the same pubertal transition at a slightly smaller size of 24 cm [Lp = 24 cm]. This minor sexual dimorphism in length at puberty implies that males may begin gametogenesis somewhat earlier than their female counterparts, a pattern observed in several other blind-snake feeding elapids. The attainment of gonadal activation represents a significant physiological milestone, after which energy allocation begins to shift from somatic growth toward the production of gametes and, eventually, offspring.

Adult females of Parasuta gouldii continue to increase in size after reaching puberty, ultimately achieving a maximum snout-vent length of 40 cm [Li = 40 cm] under favorable conditions. In contrast, males exhibit a greater ultimate length, reaching up to 46 cm [Li = up to 46 cm], a pattern of reversed sexual size dimorphism that is relatively uncommon among Australian elapids. The larger body size attained by males may confer advantages during intrasexual combat for access to receptive females, though the ecological drivers of this dimorphism remain incompletely understood. Female asymptotic mass has been recorded at 89.6 g [Wwi = 89.6 g], a value that is consistent with the species' slender build when compared to more robustly built elapids of similar length. This ultimate weight is achieved through a prolonged period of somatic investment that follows the onset of reproductive maturity. Gravid females are known to carry small clutches of two to four leathery-shelled eggs, a fecundity that is low relative to many other elapids but which may reflect the energetic constraints imposed by the species' secretive, fossorial foraging lifestyle. Reproductive output appears to be strongly tied to seasonal prey availability, with most copulations recorded during the austral spring.

The maximum lifespan documented for Parasuta gouldii under controlled laboratory conditions reaches 10 years [am = 10 years], provided the animals are maintained at a stable thermal regime of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This longevity is considerable for a snake of its size and may reflect a slow metabolic lifestyle characteristic of many fossorial or cryptozoic reptiles. The constant temperature of 28.5 °C approximates the thermal preferendum observed during the active season in the species' natural habitat, which spans the semi-arid and mediterranean-climate regions of southern Australia under logs and rocks. At this maintenance temperature, the physiological processes governing senescence appear to proceed at a measured pace, allowing individuals to reproduce across multiple seasons. Natural mortality in the wild likely occurs at a younger age due to predation by larger reptiles, birds of prey, and introduced mammalian carnivores. The interplay between thermoregulatory opportunity and longevity is particularly relevant for a species that relies on shelter-site fidelity to buffer against temperature extremes. Comparative data from related elapids suggest that the 10-year (10 years) [am = 10 years] lifespan is at the upper end of the range for small-bodied members of this family at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C].

Histological examination of reproductive tracts has clarified the timing of sexual maturation in this species, with females first exhibiting vitellogenic follicles at a body length of 25 cm [Lp = 25 cm]. Male gametogenesis, as evidenced by the presence of spermatozoa in the epididymides, commences at a snout-vent length of 24 cm [Lp = 24 cm], corroborating the earlier onset of functional maturity in males inferred from field data. The onset of puberty in both sexes appears to be more tightly correlated with body size than with chronological age, a pattern that is widespread among squamate reptiles where growth rates are highly variable across years. The 3.5 g [Wwb = 3.5 g] mass at birth provides the neonate with yolk-derived energy reserves sufficient to sustain it through the initial weeks of independent life, during which it must locate its first prey item. As juveniles grow, their diet shifts gradually from small invertebrate prey to a diet dominated by juvenile skinks, and the rate of increase in snout-vent length is most rapid during the first two years of life. Ultimately, females achieve a maximum body weight of 89.6 g [Wwi = 89.6 g], a mass that allows them to successfully gestate a clutch of eggs while maintaining sufficient energy stores for post-oviposition foraging.

Long-term captive colonies held at a constant environmental temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C] have yielded exceptional longevity records, with the oldest documented individual surviving for a full decade (10 years) [am = 10 years], a benchmark for maximum physiological longevity under optimized conditions. At this thermal regime, the metabolic demands on the animal are balanced against food intake, allowing for the maintenance of body condition well into advanced age. The asymptotic body weight of 89.6 g [Wwi = 89.6 g] recorded in captive females suggests that somatic growth in P. gouldii is largely complete by the fourth year, after which available energy is channeled primarily into reproduction rather than further increases in body mass. The 13 cm [Lb = 13 cm] hatchling snout-vent length represents an investment in relatively large offspring, a strategy that may reduce early-life mortality and set the stage for the pronounced sexual size dimorphism observed in adults, where females reach 40 cm [Li = 40 cm] and males 46 cm [Li = 46 cm]. The species' life-history strategy thus appears to be one of moderate pace: a moderately sized litter of relatively large young, a cautious growth strategy that delays reproduction until a size threshold is reached, and an extended reproductive window made possible by a long adult lifespan.
